label: Differential Forms
notes: This chapter, printed pages 349 through 376, builds the calculus of differential forms. We start from alternating tensors that measure oriented volume, assemble them with the wedge product, let them vary smoothly as forms, and crown the construction with the exterior derivative, the one operator that ties everything together.

label: Alternating Tensors
notes: A covariant k-tensor is alternating when swapping any two arguments flips the sign. The immediate consequence is that it vanishes on any linearly dependent tuple. This is the algebraic seed of orientation: alternating tensors cannot tell apart degenerate inputs, so they naturally measure signed volume rather than raw products.

label: Elementary k-Covectors and Dimension
notes: Antisymmetrizing tensor products of dual basis covectors gives elementary k-covectors indexed by increasing multi-indices. Because index order and repetition are already settled, the basis is counted by choosing k slots from n, so the dimension is the binomial coefficient. This explains why Lambda-k is small compared to the full tensor space.

label: The Wedge Product
notes: The wedge product antisymmetrizes the tensor product, producing the graded-commutative exterior algebra. The key sign rule says alpha wedge beta equals minus beta wedge alpha for one-forms, so a form wedged with itself dies. Associativity lets us build any k-covector from one-forms, which is how the basis is generated.

label: Wedge as Oriented Area
notes: Evaluate alpha wedge beta on a pair of vectors and you get the determinant of their two measurements. That determinant is exactly the signed area of the parallelogram they span. Swap the vectors and the area changes sign; feed in the same vector twice and the parallelogram collapses to zero. Forms are oriented rulers.

label: Differential Forms as Smooth Sections
notes: A differential k-form is a smooth section of the bundle of alternating k-tensors: at every point it is a k-covector, and its coefficient functions vary smoothly in coordinates. The basis monomials dx-superscript-I let us write any form, and smoothness lives entirely in those coefficient functions.

label: The Exterior Derivative
notes: The exterior derivative is the unique antiderivation that raises degree by one, reduces to the ordinary differential on functions, and squares to zero. Uniqueness is the punchline: no extra geometric data is needed, so d exists on every smooth manifold. The Leibniz rule carries a sign keyed to the degree of the first factor.

label: Coordinate Formula and d-squared
notes: In coordinates, d differentiates each coefficient and wedges with dx, antisymmetrizing automatically. Equality of mixed partials together with the antisymmetry of the wedge forces d of d to vanish. I always show students the one-form case: the curl-like coefficients reappear, and applying d again cancels in pairs.

label: Interior Multiplication
notes: Interior multiplication inserts a vector field into the first slot of a form, lowering degree by one. It is an antiderivation with a degree-keyed sign, and inserting the same vector twice gives zero. Contraction is the algebraic partner of the wedge and the second ingredient in Cartan's magic formula.

label: Pullback and Naturality
notes: Pullback moves forms backward along a smooth map, and unlike vector fields, forms always pull back without any inverse. The decisive fact is naturality: pullback commutes with the exterior derivative. This single identity is what makes integration of forms coordinate-free and powers the proof of Stokes' theorem later.

label: Closed and Exact Forms
notes: A form is closed when its exterior derivative vanishes and exact when it is itself a derivative. Because d squares to zero, every exact form is closed. The converse can fail, and the gap between closed and exact is measured by de Rham cohomology, the topological invariant this whole machinery is built to compute.

label: Grad, Curl, Divergence in R3
notes: In three dimensions the form calculus reproduces vector calculus exactly. The differential of a function is the gradient, d of a one-form encodes the curl, and d of a two-form gives the divergence. The two instances of d-squared-equals-zero become the classical identities curl of grad is zero and divergence of curl is zero.

label: Synthesis
notes: We assembled alternating algebra, then the wedge, then smooth fields, then the exterior derivative with its naturality and nilpotence. The takeaway is that one operator d unifies gradient, curl, divergence, and the boundary intuition, and the closed-versus-exact gap is the doorway to cohomology and integration on manifolds.
